frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power as a gas supplier to Europe, but export infrastructure and long-term contracts create exposure to external market pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment constraints
frictionVectors.details: Strict local-content and ownership rules protect sovereignty but can slow technology transfer and development of non-hydrocarbon resources.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt-linked infrastructure ties with China remain strategically important, limiting policy flexibility even as Luanda seeks broader partners.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and dependence on foreign operators constrain fiscal sovereignty and make diversification into critical minerals urgent.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's trade and fiscal position remain tied to port infrastructure, regional corridors, and foreign-backed investment in transport and industrial zones.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the northern borders threatens transport routes, agricultural production, and the state's ability to control frontier resources.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers bargaining tension
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence over diamond value chains, but negotiations with De Beers reflect continued dependence on external marketing and distribution networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: New mineral projects could diversify exports, although foreign capital and technical expertise may limit domestic control over emerging supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector nationalization pressure
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pushing for greater state participation and local processing of gold, challenging foreign mining firms while risking reduced investment and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Expanded security cooperation with Russia may strengthen regime autonomy, but it brings reputational, financial, and operational dependence on an external power.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Critical-Mineral Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Weak traceability and informal cross-border trade reduce state control over gold and other minerals. Regional networks linked to eastern DRC continue to challenge formal revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Rwanda constrain cross-border commerce and security coordination. External aid and diplomatic pressure remain important factors in Burundi's policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's ports and exclusive economic zone attract competing interest from European, North American, and Chinese actors. Illegal fishing and limited surveillance capacity remain persistent sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Transport, digital, and port development rely heavily on external finance and technical partners. This creates leverage for outside actors despite strong domestic institutions and generally transparent governance.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and external financing remain central to hydrocarbons, mining, and major infrastructure projects. Weak transparency and local conflict limit the state's ability to convert resource activity into broad-based sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Gulf-of-Guinea Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict disrupts transport and local economic control in the northwest and southwest. Piracy, separatist activity, and competition around the Kribi-Douala corridor add pressure to strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Presence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security support has strengthened regime protection while increasing outside influence over gold and diamond activity. Contract opacity and weak oversight limit sovereign control over mineral revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups continue to influence mining zones and trade routes outside Bangui. Poor roads and dependence on foreign security providers make national resource administration highly uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons dominate state revenues and depend on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and regional transit arrangements. Concentrated control of the sector leaves public finances vulnerable to external commercial and political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and Security Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan drives refugee flows, arms trafficking, and pressure on eastern Chad's borderlands. Continued reliance on external military and security partnerships constrains independent management of strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: French sovereignty and migration dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Mayotte dispute continues to constrain relations with France, while remittances and French-linked aid remain important to Comoros's economic stability.

frictionVectors.title: Limited control over maritime resources
frictionVectors.details: Weak enforcement capacity leaves fisheries, shipping access, and prospective offshore resources vulnerable to foreign commercial and security interests.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Rwanda-linked pressure
frictionVectors.details: M23's territorial gains and alleged external support continue to undermine Kinshasa's authority in North and South Kivu while exposing mineral corridors to coercive control.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals bargaining imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese dominance in copper and cobalt processing and expanding Western competition give Kinshasa leverage, but weak institutions limit its ability to capture full value from extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil remains central to public finance, leaving the state exposed to production volatility, foreign operators, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction support roads, urban projects, and energy infrastructure, but debt, contract opacity, and repayment through resource revenues constrain sovereign flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cocoa value capture
frictionVectors.details: State efforts to raise farmer incomes and expand local processing face entrenched influence from multinational traders, volatile prices, and compliance costs linked to European regulation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's expansion strengthens national leverage, but dependence on foreign capital and competition from ports in Ghana, Togo, and Senegal limit full control over regional logistics.

highlights: Global base hub at Bab el-Mandeb

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-base dependence
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and strategic protection but constrain Djibouti's room for maneuver amid great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and port concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port and rail projects have increased connectivity while creating debt and concession risks, particularly as Ethiopia's search for alternative maritime access intensifies.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and asset dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs and Gulf investment give outside partners influence over strategic assets, ports, and state-linked enterprises. This limits Cairo's room to retain full control over national economic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a central sovereignty and food-security concern. Water scarcity and dependence on upstream cooperation increase Egypt's strategic vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas output is reducing fiscal autonomy while the state remains heavily dependent on hydrocarbons. Foreign operators and lenders retain leverage over remaining projects and monetization infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and energy projects have expanded infrastructure but increased exposure to external contractors, debt obligations, and opaque resource-linked arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to Yemen place it inside intensifying regional competition over ports, shipping, and military access. External security actors could pressure Asmara despite its preference for strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining remains one of the few major sources of foreign exchange and is concentrated among external partners. Limited transparency and sanctions exposure constrain the state's ability to capture and diversify resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African trade, transport links, energy systems, and customs revenues. This dependence limits independent control over supply chains and exposes the kingdom to regional economic shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent governance criticism and demands for reform create openings for external diplomatic and commercial influence. Fiscal constraints make infrastructure and development financing increasingly dependent on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and regional tensions
frictionVectors.details: The GERD has strengthened Ethiopia's leverage over electricity and Nile diplomacy, but unresolved disputes with Egypt and Sudan continue to carry escalation risks. Water negotiations remain intertwined with broader Red Sea competition.

frictionVectors.title: External financing constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF-linked reforms, and reliance on foreign investment constrain Addis Ababa's policy autonomy. Conflict-related insecurity also threatens transport corridors, industrial projects, and domestic resource mobilization.

frictionVectors.title: French Economic Footprint
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater national control over oil, mining, and strategic infrastructure while renegotiating relationships long shaped by French firms and networks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Chinese Financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and infrastructure dependence could expand Chinese leverage, particularly around mining logistics, rail, and port development.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, energy connectivity, and regional security, limiting its room for independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Fisheries Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Banjul's port modernization and fisheries sector remain vulnerable to external commercial influence, opaque licensing, and weak enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage water systems, farmland, and state authority while linking local actors to international gold-processing and trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in lithium, bauxite, and manganese is increasing, but fiscal stress may push Accra toward contracts that provide limited domestic processing or technology transfer.

highlights: Military Rule Trades Access for Stability

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Consortium Competition
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is drawing major Chinese and other foreign capital, giving outside partners substantial influence over rail, port, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Legitimacy Crisis
frictionVectors.details: The authorities use mining expansion to bolster revenues and legitimacy, while political restrictions and delayed civilian transition increase regional and investor risk.

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine Transit Networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime surveillance leave the country vulnerable to transnational trafficking networks that erode sovereign control and influence elite politics.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Cashew Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and regional operators dominate cashew trade and port logistics, limiting domestic value capture and increasing exposure to political disruption.

highlights: Port and energy corridors remain strategic

frictionVectors.title: External debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy repayment obligations to commercial, Chinese, and multilateral lenders constrain Nairobi's ability to set infrastructure and fiscal policy independently.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the LAPSSET corridor remain exposed to competition and external financing pressure from Gulf, Chinese, and regional interests.

highlights: Water exports deepen South African dependence

frictionVectors.title: Water-for-revenue asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital income but leaves the kingdom structurally dependent on South Africa for its main export market, infrastructure, and security environment.

frictionVectors.title: Hydropower financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large water and energy projects rely on external lenders and contractors, limiting local control over project terms and long-term revenue capture.

highlights: Ports and concessions remain externally shaped

frictionVectors.title: Mineral concession concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and gold projects generate employment and fiscal receipts but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and weak domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Concession arrangements around ports, roads, and major industrial assets give external firms substantial influence over logistics and revenue flows.

highlights: Foreign patrons compete through security networks

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks contest control over fields, export terminals, and budget flows, weakening the National Oil Corporation's ability to enforce unified sovereign policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, and other regional powers retain leverage through security partnerships, bases, arms, and political alliances tied to energy and maritime interests.

frictionVectors.title: Mining enclave dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains, with limited domestic refining and value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and power vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity and transport deficits increase reliance on external financiers and operators, reducing Antananarivo's leverage in negotiating resource concessions.

frictionVectors.title: MINING GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms are positioning around uranium, graphite and rare-earth prospects while Malawi still lacks the financing and regulatory capacity to secure strong domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and dependence on imported fuel expose the country to external lenders, suppliers and infrastructure operators.

highlights: Junta prioritizes sovereign control of gold
Security dependence is shifting toward Russia

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SECTOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is tightening taxation and state participation in mining, but foreign operators, informal production and opaque security-linked arrangements continue to limit effective national control.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces has increased reliance on Russian-linked security support, while militant attacks threaten transport corridors, mining zones and state reach.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers new revenues and regional influence, but foreign operators and export infrastructure retain substantial control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports depend heavily on the national railway and port system, leaving Mauritania vulnerable to external financing conditions, commodity cycles and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The long-running dispute over the Chagos Archipelago and Diego Garcia remains central to Mauritius's territorial sovereignty, despite diplomatic progress toward a negotiated settlement.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND FINANCE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius seeks to expand maritime logistics and ocean resources while balancing dependence on foreign capital, shipping networks and competing Indian Ocean powers.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCES
frictionVectors.details: Control and development of Western Sahara remain contested internationally, creating legal and diplomatic exposure for phosphate, fisheries, energy and infrastructure projects.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Major ports, railways and renewable-energy projects strengthen Moroccan autonomy but also increase strategic competition among European, Gulf, Chinese and American partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Gas development depends heavily on foreign capital, contractors, and security support, limiting Mozambique's near-term control over strategic energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks and displacement continue to threaten transport corridors, project timelines, and state authority in the LNG-producing north.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in New Energy
frictionVectors.details: Green-hydrogen and offshore petroleum projects could expand state revenues, but financing, technology, and marketing remain dominated by external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic power generation, water availability, and port capacity could reduce Namibia's bargaining power with major investors and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Niamey's push to renegotiate or reclaim greater control over uranium assets has sharpened tensions with established foreign operators and exposed export vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Insecurity and strained relations with neighbors threaten crude-export infrastructure, commercial access, and the junta's ability to convert resource control into stable revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Theft and Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, illegal refining, and pipeline attacks continue to erode public revenues and weaken Nigeria's effective control over petroleum infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Fiscal Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking greater domestic processing and local content, but upstream investment, technology, and foreign-exchange pressures still constrain sovereign policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's alleged support for M23 and its role in regional mineral networks continue to trigger diplomatic pressure, sanctions risks, and scrutiny of cross-border supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Reputation Risk
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's ambition to become a formal minerals-processing and trading hub is constrained by traceability concerns and dependence on regional supply routes.

frictionVectors.title: Unproven offshore hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe retains legal control over prospective offshore blocks, but lacks the capital and technical capacity to develop them independently. Licensing decisions remain vulnerable to pressure from foreign energy companies and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and investment provide useful infrastructure but increase long-term financial and political dependence. Maritime security and fisheries enforcement also rely heavily on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led offshore production
frictionVectors.details: Sangomar and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim production offer Senegal new leverage, but operations remain dependent on foreign operators, technology, and financing. The government is pressing for greater local content and improved revenue capture without disrupting output.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and renegotiation constraints
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stress limits Dakar's room to renegotiate mining, energy, and infrastructure agreements. Tensions with international lenders could constrain the government's sovereignty-focused economic program.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of maritime capacity
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on external partners for surveillance, patrol assets, and maritime-domain awareness across its vast exclusive economic zone. Indian, European, and other security relationships require careful balancing to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and tourism dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing fleets and tourism investors remain central to revenue generation, limiting domestic control over key blue-economy assets. Climate exposure and external financing needs further narrow policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-linked mineral dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects rely heavily on foreign capital, operators, and logistics networks. Sierra Leone gains export revenue but remains exposed to opaque contracts, commodity-price swings, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, rail, and mining infrastructure can improve connectivity while giving external firms influence over strategic export corridors. Weak fiscal capacity complicates efforts to secure stronger local ownership and processing commitments.

frictionVectors.title: Petroleum authority dispute
frictionVectors.details: Offshore licensing and revenue-sharing remain entangled in disputes between the federal government and member states. Foreign exploration partners may gain leverage from institutional fragmentation and unresolved petroleum governance.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and port rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors compete for influence over ports, security partnerships, and logistics access. This investment can strengthen state capacity but also risks turning infrastructure into a channel for geopolitical dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial geological and industrial leverage, but foreign capital and downstream-processing gaps limit sovereign control over platinum-group metals, manganese and rare-earth supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, port congestion and rail deterioration constrain mineral exports and create openings for external financiers and operators to shape infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's export revenues depend on pipelines and terminals outside its territory, leaving production and fiscal sovereignty exposed to Sudan's conflict, transit politics and external commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Armed political fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Elite competition, subnational violence and delayed political reforms weaken state control over oil regions, border corridors and prospective mineral assets.

highlights: Gold and ports draw external competition

frictionVectors.title: Gold-war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival armed networks, while foreign buyers and regional intermediaries capture value beyond effective civilian state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime facilities and transport corridors are strategic prizes for external powers seeking influence over Sudan's coastline and future trade flows.

highlights: LNG and rail corridors advance cautiously

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater domestic value from offshore gas, but negotiations with international energy firms and financing constraints shape the pace and terms of development.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is tightening local-processing and fiscal rules for mining, creating periodic tension with foreign investors over licensing, ownership and export controls.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a Gulf of Guinea logistics hub generates leverage, but dependence on foreign shipping, finance and security networks limits fully autonomous control of trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate value-chain gap
frictionVectors.details: Togo controls a significant phosphate resource base but remains constrained by capital, processing capacity and external market conditions in converting reserves into broader sovereign industrial power.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia's strained public finances and limited access to concessional funding increase dependence on European support and bilateral lenders. Financing negotiations remain closely tied to migration management and economic reform.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: High reliance on imported hydrocarbons constrains fiscal and strategic autonomy. Delays in renewable-energy investment and persistent utility losses deepen vulnerability to external price and supply shocks.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces environmental, legal, and financing pressure from foreign governments and institutions. Its dependence on external construction, insurance, and markets limits full national control over oil monetization.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign lenders and contractors retain a major role in roads, power, and industrial infrastructure. Debt-servicing obligations and project terms create long-term leverage over national development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership Competition
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking greater state participation and revenue capture while courting Western, Gulf, and Chinese investors for mine expansion. Competition over taxation, local processing, and strategic control remains intense.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Power Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved fiscal room but leaves Zambia exposed to creditor conditions and market confidence. Electricity shortages and dependence on regional power imports threaten copper output and weaken bargaining power with investors.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Externalization
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate financing, technology, and market access for lithium, platinum, gold, and other minerals. Export restrictions and beneficiation demands have increased state leverage, but opaque licensing and limited domestic capacity constrain effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Payment Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Targeted sanctions, arrears, and restricted access to international finance raise transaction costs and push the government toward alternative lenders and politically aligned investors. This narrows choices while increasing dependence on opaque bilateral and commercial arrangements.
